quote.after:
For the absolutely continuous curve conclusion (c), assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) as required by the cited causal-curve calculus and fundamental theorem. The other clauses use the given smooth observer structure, pointwise adapted-chart existence and finite compactness arguments, without these additional curve-calculus premises. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), and put $n=N/\sqrt{-g(N,N)}$. Write $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. In a chart $(U,x)$ put $v^a=dx^a(v)$, $v_s=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and $|v|_{\mathrm e}=(\sum_{a=0}^3(v^a)^2)^{1/2}$.

**(a) Adapted orthonormal charts.** For every $p\in M$ there are a chart $(U,x)$, $x(p)=0$, a radius $r>0$ with $U=x^{-1}(B_r)$, and $K\ge1$, such that on all of $U$
$$n=\partial_{x^0},\qquad g_{00}\equiv-1,\qquad g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}.$$

**(b) Cone domination.** The chart and radius in (a) can be chosen so every nonzero future causal vector at any point of $U$ satisfies
$$|v_s|\le K v^0,\qquad |v^i|\le K v^0\quad(i=1,2,3),\qquad v^0\ge K^{-1}|v|_{\mathrm e}>0.$$

**(c) Curve form.** Every future causal curve $\gamma:I\to U$ of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] has strictly increasing time coordinate, and for all $s<t$ in $I$
$$x^0(\gamma(s))<x^0(\gamma(t)),\qquad |x_s(\gamma(t))-x_s(\gamma(s))|\le K\left(x^0(\gamma(t))-x^0(\gamma(s))\right).$$
Consequently every spatial component satisfies the same bound, and the curve image is the graph of a $K$-Lipschitz function into Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ over the interval $x^0(\gamma(I))$.

**(d) Flat minorant cone.** The same chart can be chosen so the constant-coordinate metric $\eta_{16}=-(dx^0)^2+16\sum_i(dx^i)^2$ has every nonzero $\eta_{16}$-causal vector $g$-timelike throughout $U$. If $q,q'\in U$ and $\eta_{16}(x(q')-x(q),x(q')-x(q))<0$, then $q\ll q'$ if $x^0(q')>x^0(q)$, and $q'\ll q$ otherwise.

**(e) General temporal charts: exact compact uniformity.** For any chart $(U',z)$ define its temporal locus
$$P=\{q\in U':\nabla z^0(q)\text{ is past timelike}\}.$$
For every compact set $K_0\subset P$ there is $L\ge1$ such that all nonzero future causal vectors based in $K_0$, with coordinate components and Euclidean norm taken in $z$, satisfy
$$|v_s|\le L v^0,\qquad |v^i|\le L v^0,\qquad v^0\ge L^{-1}|v|_{\mathrm e}>0.$$
In particular these bounds hold throughout any relatively compact $U_0\Subset U'$ whose closure is contained in $P$, equivalently whose time gradient is past timelike on its entire closure. Timelikeness merely on $U_0$ gives local bounds at each point and uniform bounds on each compact subset of $U_0$; it does not alone give a uniform bound on all of $U_0$.

No additional choice is used to select the pointwise linear bases or compact cone constants. Countable and Dependent Choice are explicitly required only for the general absolutely continuous curve clause (c), through its actual calculus suppliers.

after.claim: (Clause (a).) By [L1] the set $A$ is closed and achronal. If a timelike curve $\gamma$ met $A$ at two distinct parameter values $s<s'$, then $\gamma|_{[s,s']}$ would be a future timelike curve from $\gamma(s)$ to $\gamma(s')$ (or a past one after reversing), so the two points of $A$ would be chronologically related, contradicting achronality; hence at most one meeting.

(Points of $F$ and of its complement near $p$.) Since $p\in A=\partial F$ we have $p\in\overline F$ and $p\notin F$. By [L2] applied to the future set $F$, every $r\in I^+(p)$ lies in $F$. Moreover every $r\in I^-(p)$ lies outside $\overline F$: otherwise $r\in\overline F$ and $p\in I^+(r)$, so [L2] would give $p\in F$, a contradiction.

(Nearby points of $F$ and of $M\setminus\overline F$ on every vertical line.) Let $(U,x)$, $K$, $c$ be as in [L3]. Choose $a,\rho>0$ with $\sqrt{a^2+\rho^2}$ smaller than the radius of $U$ and $\sqrt c\,\rho+1<a$; then the box $W=x^{-1}\bigl((-a,a)\times B_\rho(0)\bigr)$ is contained in $U$. For $z\in B_\rho(0)$ put $q^+_z:=x^{-1}(\sqrt c\,|z|+1,z)$ and $q^-_z:=x^{-1}(-\sqrt c\,|z|-1,z)$, both in $W$. Computing in the flat form, $$\eta_c\bigl(q^+_z-p,q^+_z-p\bigr)=-\bigl(\sqrt c\,|z|+1\bigr)^2+c|z|^2=-2\sqrt c\,|z|-1<0,$$ and likewise $\eta_c(q^-_z-p,q^-_z-p)=-2\sqrt c\,|z|-1<0$. By [L3] (clause (d)) we get $p\ll q^+_z$ and $q^-_z\ll p$; with step 1.2 this gives $q^+_z\in F$ and $q^-_z\notin\overline F$.

(Existence of a boundary point on each vertical line.) Fix $z\in B_\rho(0)$ and let $S_z$ be the coordinate subsegment of $L_z$ joining $q^-_z$ to $q^+_z$. The map $s\mapsto x^{-1}(s,z)$ is continuous, so $S_z$ is connected; it contains $q^+_z\in F$ and $q^-_z\in M\setminus\overline F\subseteq M\setminus F$. Since $F$ is open in $M$, the connected set $S_z$ cannot be covered by the two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets $S_z\cap F$ and $S_z\cap\mathrm{Int}(M\setminus F)$ without meeting the complement of their union, which is $A$; hence $A\cap S_z\neq\emptyset$.

(Uniqueness of the boundary point on a vertical line.) Let $r,r'\in A\cap L_z$ be distinct, say $r=x^{-1}(s,z)$ and $r'=x^{-1}(s',z)$ with $s<s'$; by [L4] $r\ll r'$, contradicting the achronality of $A$ from step 1.1. Hence $A\cap L_z$ has at most one point, and by step 3.1 exactly one.

(The graphing function.) For $z\in B_\rho(0)$ let $\varphi(z)\in(-a,a)$ be the $x^0$-coordinate of the unique point of $A\cap L_z$; it is well defined by step 4.1, and since the unique point of $A\cap L_z$ found in step 3.1 lies between $q^-_z$ and $q^+_z$ we have $|\varphi(z)|\le\sqrt c\,|z|+1<a$. Then $$A\cap W=\{x^{-1}(\varphi(z),z):z\in B_\rho(0)\},$$ because the inclusion $\supseteq$ holds by definition of $\varphi$, and if $x^{-1}(s,z)\in A\cap W$ then this point lies on $L_z$ and uniqueness forces $s=\varphi(z)$.

(Lipschitz bound.) Let $z,z'\in B_\rho(0)$ and suppose $|\varphi(z)-\varphi(z')|>\sqrt c\,|z-z'|$. Put $\delta:=(\varphi(z)-\varphi(z'),z-z')$ and assume $\varphi(z)>\varphi(z')$, the other case being symmetric. Then $\eta_c(\delta,\delta)=-(\varphi(z)-\varphi(z'))^2+c|z-z'|^2<0$, and both $x^{-1}(\varphi(z),z)$ and $x^{-1}(\varphi(z'),z')$ lie in $A\cap W\subseteq U$, so [L3] (clause (d)) gives $x^{-1}(\varphi(z'),z')\ll x^{-1}(\varphi(z),z)$, two distinct points of $A$ chronologically related, contradicting step 1.1. Hence $|\varphi(z)-\varphi(z')|\le\sqrt c|z-z'|$.

(Clause (c).) The map $\psi:B_\rho(0)\to A\cap W$, $\psi(z):=x^{-1}(\varphi(z),z)$, is continuous because $\varphi$ is Lipschitz by step 6.1 and $x^{-1}$ is continuous; it is bijective onto $A\cap W$ by step 5.1. The restriction of the continuous projection $\pi:x^{-1}(s,z)\mapsto z$ to $A\cap W$ is its inverse: for $r\in A\cap W$ we have $r=x^{-1}(\varphi(\pi(r)),\pi(r))$ by step 4.1, so $\psi(\pi(r))=r$, and $\pi$ is continuous. Hence $\psi$ is a homeomorphism onto the relatively open set $A\cap W$. For two such graph charts $\psi:B_\rho(0)\to A\cap W$ and $\psi':B_{\rho'}(0)\to A\cap W'$ coming from charts $x,x'$, the transition $\psi'^{-1}\circ\psi$ equals $\pi'\circ\psi$ on $\psi^{-1}(A\cap W\cap W')$, a composition of continuous maps; hence the graph parametrizations form a topological atlas on $A$, making $A$ a topological $3$-manifold and the inclusion $A\hookrightarrow M$ a topological embedding.

(Clause (d).) Assume countable choice and let $K\subseteq M$ be compact; then $A\cap K$ is compact because $A$ is closed. Cover $A\cap K$ by finitely many graph neighborhoods $W_1,\dots,W_m$ as in (b), with charts $x_j$ and graphing functions $\varphi_j$ defined on the balls $B_{\rho_j}(0)$. In the chart $x_j$ the set $A\cap W_j$ is contained in the graph of $\varphi_j$, which is the graph of the measurable function obtained by extending $\varphi_j$ by zero outside $B_{\rho_j}(0)$: that extension is continuous on the open ball and constant on its complement, hence Borel measurable by [L5]. By [L5] the graph has four-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero, so the coordinate image of $A\cap W_j$ is Lebesgue null, and the local absolute continuity of $\mu$ gives $\mu(A\cap W_j)=0$; here $A\cap W_j$ is Borel because $A$ is closed. By finite additivity and $A\cap K\subseteq\bigcup_j(A\cap W_j)$, $\mu(A\cap K)=0$. This proves (d).
